440358154.name: Communities: How can we better understand and respect people with disabilities?
440358154.description: This unit helps pupils respect people with disabilities. Pupils explore disability concepts, experiences in modern Britain, the Equality Act 2010 and the Paralympics, developing practical skills to promote inclusive attitudes in their school and wider community.
440358154.why: This unit builds on prior learning about respect and kindness by focusing specifically on disability, a crucial protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010. Positioned at the start of secondary school, it deepens pupils' understanding of inclusivity and discrimination, preparing them for future RSHE discussions about equality, diversity and respectful relationships.
prior: Pupils should have a basic understanding of respect and kindness in relationships from Key Stage 2, recognising that everyone is different and deserves to be treated fairly.
Pupils should be familiar with the concept of diversity within their primary school community and understand that treating others with dignity is important.
Pupils should be able to identify when someone is being unkind or excluded and recognise that discrimination is wrong, having encountered these ideas in primary education.

365770270.name: Healthy relationships: How can I build good relationships?
365770270.description: This unit explores the characteristics of healthy friendships and strategies for making new friends. Pupils understand why friendships are important for wellbeing, learn how friendships change over time, and develop practical skills for managing friendship transitions respectfully.
365770270.why: This unit supports pupils during their transition to secondary school by equipping them with essential friendship-building skills for new social environments. Positioned at the start of Year 7, it provides a foundation for understanding healthy relationships that will be built upon throughout their RSHE curriculum. At this developmental stage, pupils are forming new peer groups and often require practical strategies for communication, conflict resolution and maintaining positive relationships.
prior: Pupils should understand basic concepts of kindness and fairness in relationships from Key Stage 2, recognising that treating others well is important for maintaining friendships.
Pupils should be familiar with identifying their own feelings and understanding that disagreements with friends are normal and can be resolved through communication.
Pupils should have experience of working cooperatively with others in primary school and understand that different people have different interests, personalities and communication styles.

898083113.name: Power in relationships: How can we create positive relationships?
898083113.description: This unit explores positive relationships and their benefits. Pupils understand their role in creating respectful interactions, recognise power dynamics, and learn how happiness, self-respect and mutual respect underpin healthy, balanced relationships.
898083113.why: This unit builds directly on the previous 'Healthy relationships' unit by helping pupils understand power dynamics within their new secondary school peer groups. At this developmental stage, pupils are increasingly influenced by peers and need skills to recognise and respond to power imbalances respectfully. This foundational knowledge prepares pupils for more complex discussions about consent, equality and respectful relationships later in their RSHE curriculum.
prior: Pupils should understand basic friendship skills from the previous unit, including communication, respect and kindness, and recognise the characteristics of positive relationships.
Pupils should be able to identify their own feelings and understand that people can influence each other's choices and behaviour in both positive and negative ways.
Pupils should have a basic understanding from Key Stage 2 that some people may have more power or authority than others, such as adults, teachers or older pupils.

583594469.name: Media influence: How can I evaluate the truth online?
583594469.description: This unit develops critical evaluation skills for assessing online content. Pupils learn to identify misinformation, understand how fake news spreads, explore influencer culture and motivations, and recognise the real-world consequences of believing and sharing false information.
583594469.why: By Year 7, most pupils will be using online content as an information source. This unit equips them with essential critical thinking skills to navigate digital information safely and responsibly. Positioned early in secondary school, it provides foundational media literacy that underpins all subsequent online safety and health education, enabling pupils to make informed decisions about the content they consume and share.
prior: Pupils should understand from Key Stage 2 that not everything online is true and that they should ask a trusted adult if they're unsure about online content or information.
Pupils should be familiar with using the internet for research and communication, and understand that people share information and opinions online through social media and websites.
Pupils should recognise from previous units that people can present themselves differently online than in person, and that online interactions follow the same expectations as offline.

525523093.name: Our online lives: How do I report and find support for things I see online?
525523093.description: This unit helps pupils navigate online safety by recognising harmful content, understanding when and how to report concerns, and accessing appropriate support. Pupils explore both the benefits and risks of online activity whilst learning their role in creating safer digital communities.
525523093.why: As Year 7 pupils become increasingly independent online, they need practical skills to identify and respond to harmful content appropriately. This unit provides essential safeguarding knowledge, teaching pupils when and how to report concerns and access support. Positioned early in secondary school, it establishes clear reporting procedures and reinforces that seeking help is responsible, not troublesome, creating a foundation for safe digital citizenship throughout their teenage years.
prior: Pupils should understand basic online safety rules, including not sharing personal information with strangers and telling a trusted adult if something makes them uncomfortable.
Pupils should be familiar with common online platforms and activities such as social media, gaming and messaging, and understand that online actions have real-world consequences.
Pupils should recognise from previous units that not all online content is true or safe, and that people can behave differently online than they would face-to-face.

46184780.name: Staying safe and healthy: How do I maintain physical health?
46184780.description: This unit covers the fundamentals of maintaining physical health. Pupils learn how germs spread and how to prevent infection, recognise symptoms of common illnesses and when to seek help, and understand the importance of dental hygiene for long-term health.
46184780.why: As pupils transition to secondary school, they develop greater independence in managing their personal health and hygiene. This unit equips them with practical knowledge to prevent illness, treat minor ailments independently, and understand when professional help is needed. Positioned early in Year 7, it establishes healthy habits and personal responsibility for wellbeing that will support them throughout adolescence and into adulthood.
prior: Pupils should understand from Key Stage 2 basic hygiene practices such as handwashing, covering coughs and sneezes, and that keeping clean helps prevent illness and infection.
Pupils should know that there are different types of illnesses and that some require rest at home whilst others need medical attention from a doctor or healthcare professional.
Pupils should be familiar with basic dental care from primary school, including brushing teeth regularly, and understand that dentists help maintain healthy teeth and gums.

460842153.name: Physical health: Why have a healthy diet?
460842153.description: This unit emphasises the importance of maintaining a healthy, balanced diet for physical wellbeing. Pupils explore the links between diet, exercise and health, learn about nutritional choices, and understand how healthy habits support growth, energy and long-term health.
460842153.why: As Year 7 pupils gain independence, they increasingly make their own food choices and establish habits that will last into adulthood. This unit provides essential knowledge about nutrition, the relationship between diet and health, and the importance of physical activity. Positioned early in secondary school, it empowers pupils to make informed decisions that support their growth, energy levels and long-term physical and mental wellbeing during an important developmental period.
prior: Pupils should understand from Key Stage 2 that eating a variety of foods including fruits, vegetables, protein and carbohydrates is important for a healthy, balanced diet.
Pupils should know that regular physical activity is important for staying healthy and that different activities help keep the body strong and fit.
Pupils should be familiar with basic concepts of healthy living from previous units, including that personal choices about diet and exercise affect overall wellbeing.

765247282.name: Mental health: How can I talk about my feelings?
765247282.description: This unit develops emotional literacy and communication skills. Pupils learn to identify and articulate their feelings, develop active listening skills, and manage conflict constructively. The unit emphasises that emotions are normal and provides practical strategies for effective communication.
765247282.why: As Year 7 pupils navigate new social environments and academic pressures in secondary school, they require emotional literacy skills to express their feelings and seek support effectively. This unit provides essential vocabulary and strategies for understanding emotions, communicating needs and managing conflicts respectfully. Positioned early in Year 7, it establishes a foundation for mental wellbeing and positive relationships that supports all future RSHE learning and personal development.
prior: Pupils should understand from Key Stage 2 that everyone experiences different emotions and that feelings can change throughout the day or in different situations.
Pupils should know basic emotion vocabulary such as happy, sad, angry, worried or excited, and recognise that talking about feelings with trusted adults can help when upset.
Pupils should be familiar from previous units with the importance of treating others with respect and kindness, and understand that disagreements are a normal part of relationships.

280709529.name: Risky substances: What do I need to know about tobacco and vaping?
280709529.description: This unit explores the serious health risks of smoking, vaping and nicotine products. Pupils learn why these substances are harmful, understand their impact on physical and mental health, develop strategies to resist pressure, and know how to access support for quitting.
280709529.why: As Year 7 pupils encounter increased peer influence and exposure to tobacco and vaping through social circles and media, they need accurate information to make informed choices. This unit provides essential health education about the serious risks of smoking and vaping, equips pupils with refusal skills, and normalises seeking support. Positioned early in Key Stage 3, it aims to prevent experimentation during a critical period when habits form, protecting pupils' long-term physical and mental health.
prior: Pupils should understand from Key Stage 2 that smoking is harmful to health and that breathing in smoke from cigarettes can damage the lungs and body.
Pupils should know basic strategies for saying no to peer pressure from previous units, including being confident in their own choices and seeking support from trusted adults.
Pupils should be familiar with accessing healthcare support from previous health units, understanding that doctors, nurses and other professionals can provide help and advice.

19775004.name: Our changing bodies: What do I need to know about menstruation?
19775004.description: This unit provides essential information about menstrual health and wellbeing. Pupils learn what menstruation is, how to manage periods, understand the emotional changes that can occur, and know when to seek professional support.
19775004.why: As Year 7 pupils experience or approach puberty, they need accurate, appropriate information about menstruation to reduce anxiety and dispel myths. This unit provides essential knowledge about menstrual health, practical management strategies, and emotional wellbeing during periods. Positioned early in Key Stage 3, it ensures all pupils understand this natural process, can manage it confidently and hygienically, and know when to seek professional support, promoting positive attitudes towards menstrual health.
prior: Pupils should understand from Key Stage 2 that puberty is a natural process involving physical and emotional changes, and that these changes happen at different times for different people.
Pupils should know basic information about the human body and reproductive system, including that menstruation is a normal part of female development.
Pupils should be familiar from previous units with talking about feelings and emotions, and understand that seeking help from healthcare professionals is important when needed.

837004842.name: Communities: How do we respect people of different faiths?
837004842.description: This unit explores how to respect people of different faiths by examining the role of faith in communities and its influence on culture in modern Britain. Pupils learn to challenge prejudice, promote inclusivity, demonstrate kindness and stay safe in community spaces.
837004842.why: This unit deepens Year 8 pupils' understanding of diversity by focusing on faith and religion, key protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010. Building on Year 7 learning about respect and inclusion, pupils develop more sophisticated understanding of prejudice and discrimination based on religion or belief.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 7 that everyone deserves respect and dignity, including people with protected characteristics such as religion, and that discrimination is wrong.
Pupils should be familiar with the concept of diversity and inclusion from previous units, recognising that communities are made up of people with different backgrounds and beliefs.
Pupils should know from earlier learning about stereotypes and prejudice, understanding that assumptions based on someone's identity or background can cause harm and should be challenged.

430048914.name: Healthy relationships: Why should we prevent bullying?
430048914.description: This unit examines different types of bullying and their impact on individuals and communities. Pupils learn to recognise bullying behaviours, understand bystander responsibilities, develop strategies to challenge and stop bullying, and know how to access support.
430048914.why: As Year 8 pupils navigate increasingly complex peer relationships and greater online independence, they require sophisticated understanding of bullying dynamics and power imbalances. This unit builds on Year 7 relationship knowledge by examining bystander responsibility and active intervention strategies. At this developmental stage, pupils can understand the serious impact of bullying on mental health and wellbeing, empowering them to create safer, more supportive communities both online and offline.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 7 what constitutes respectful behaviour in relationships and that bullying, both online and offline, is harmful and unacceptable.
Pupils should be familiar with identifying harmful online behaviours from previous units, including recognising when social media or technology is used to hurt or control others.
Pupils should know from earlier learning how to report concerns to trusted adults and understand that seeking help for themselves or others is a responsible action.

21354892.name: Power in relationships: What do we need to know about the law?
21354892.description: This unit explores the legal aspects of harmful sexual behaviour, including sexual harassment and image-based abuse. Pupils learn what the law says, how to protect themselves online, recognise exploitation such as sextortion, and know how to seek support and report concerns.
21354892.why: As Year 8 pupils navigate increasingly independent online and social lives, they need clear understanding of the legal boundaries around sexual behaviour and image sharing. This unit provides essential safeguarding knowledge about what constitutes harmful sexual behaviour, the serious legal consequences, and how to protect themselves and others. At this developmental stage, pupils can understand these complex legal concepts, empowering them to recognise exploitation, report concerns confidently, and build safe, respectful relationships.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 7 what constitutes respectful behaviour in relationships, including the importance of consent, kindness and boundaries in all interactions.
Pupils should be familiar with online safety principles from previous units, including not sharing personal information or images, and recognising when online behaviour becomes harmful.
Pupils should know from earlier learning how to report concerns and access support, understanding that harmful behaviour is never the victim's fault and help is always available.

866129914.name: Media influence: What's a healthy way to spend my time online?
866129914.description: This unit explores the impact of online time on wellbeing, including effects on sleep, body image, self-esteem and learning. Pupils learn to recognise healthy and unhealthy online habits, understand how curated content affects them, and develop practical strategies for balanced digital lives.
866129914.why: As Year 8 pupils spend increasing time online and on social media, they need to understand how digital habits impact their wellbeing, self-image and academic performance. This unit provides essential knowledge about the effects of excessive screen time, curated online content and unhealthy comparisons. At this developmental stage, pupils are particularly vulnerable to online pressures around body image and self-worth, making it crucial they develop balanced digital habits and critical awareness to protect their own self-worth and maintain healthy offline lives.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 7 that online content can present distorted pictures of reality and that not everything shared online is true or represents real life accurately.
Pupils should be familiar with basic online safety and digital wellbeing concepts from previous units, including the importance of balancing screen time with other activities.
Pupils should know from earlier learning about the benefits of physical activity, sleep and spending time with others for mental and physical health and overall wellbeing.

45576582.name: Our online lives: How can I stay safe?
45576582.description: This unit addresses online bullying, exploring why it happens, its impact on victims and communities, and effective response strategies. Pupils learn to identify harmful online behaviours, understand their responsibilities as bystanders, and develop practical skills for maintaining safety.
45576582.why: As Year 8 pupils engage more independently with online spaces, they face increased risks of encountering or experiencing cyberbullying. This unit provides essential knowledge about online bullying dynamics, including why people behave differently online and how conflicts escalate digitally. At this developmental stage, pupils need practical strategies to protect themselves, support peers, and respond effectively to online threats, ensuring they can navigate digital spaces safely and maintain their wellbeing and positive online communities.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 7 what constitutes bullying and harmful online behaviour, including that cyberbullying is unacceptable and has serious consequences for victims.
Pupils should be familiar with how to report concerns and access support from previous units, understanding that reporting is a responsible action that helps protect themselves and others.
Pupils should know from earlier learning about respectful online communication and that social media behaviour should follow the same standards as face-to-face interactions.

94065365.name: Physical health: Why stay active?
94065365.description: This unit emphasises the importance of physical activity for health and wellbeing. Pupils explore practical strategies for staying active, understand the physical and mental health benefits of regular exercise, and learn how active lifestyles support wellbeing.
94065365.why: As Year 8 pupils experience continued physical and emotional changes during adolescence, they need to understand how regular physical activity supports their development, mental health and academic performance. This unit provides practical strategies for maintaining active lifestyles through adolesence. At this developmental stage, establishing exercise habits is crucial for long-term health, resilience and wellbeing throughout adolescence and into adulthood.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 7 that regular physical activity is important for maintaining a healthy body.
Pupils should be familiar with the links between diet, exercise and health from previous units, recognising that lifestyle choices affect both physical and mental wellbeing.
Pupils should know from earlier learning about the importance of sleep, time outdoors and balanced lifestyles for maintaining good health and supporting growth during adolescence.

648340108.name: Mental health: How can I support my mental health?
648340108.description: This unit explores strategies for supporting mental health and wellbeing. Pupils learn how talking helps mental health, understand factors that influence it, develop skills for managing emotions, and practise calming and relaxation techniques to build resilience.
648340108.why: As Year 8 pupils face increasing academic and social pressures during adolescence, they need practical strategies to support their mental health and build resilience. This unit provides essential skills for emotional regulation, stress management and seeking support when needed. At this developmental stage, pupils can understand mental health as something everyone experiences and maintains, empowering them to develop healthy habits that will support their wellbeing throughout adolescence and beyond.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 7 that everyone experiences different emotions and that worrying or feeling down are normal responses that can affect anyone at different times.
Pupils should be familiar with talking about feelings using appropriate vocabulary from previous units, and recognise that discussing emotions with trusted people can help manage them.
Pupils should know about common mental health concerns such as anxiety and stress, and understand that seeking support from adults or professionals is important and helpful.

326837817.name: Staying safe and healthy: What do I need to know about minor ailments?
326837817.description: This unit covers recognising and managing common minor ailments. Pupils learn about treating coughs, colds and flu, responding to rashes, bites, stings and allergic reactions, and managing stomach illnesses, including when to seek professional help.
326837817.why: As Year 8 pupils gain greater independence in managing their health, they need practical knowledge to recognise and treat common minor ailments confidently. This unit empowers pupils to distinguish between illnesses they can self-manage and those requiring professional help. At this developmental stage, understanding how to access healthcare support appropriately and treat minor conditions independently builds confidence.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 7 basic hygiene practices such as handwashing and covering coughs, and that keeping clean helps prevent the spread of germs and illness.
Pupils should be familiar with basic first aid and self-care from previous units, including when minor ailments can be treated at home and when professional medical help is needed.
Pupils should know from earlier learning about the role of healthcare professionals such as pharmacists, GPs and nurses in providing advice and treatment for common health concerns.

626074834.name: Risky substances: What do I need to know about alcohol?
626074834.description: This unit examines the laws around alcohol, its physical and mental health effects, and strategies for staying safe. Pupils learn about legal restrictions, understand the risks of alcohol consumption, and develop skills to make informed, safe decisions.
626074834.why: As Year 8 pupils may begin encountering alcohol in social situations, they need accurate information about legal restrictions, health risks and safety strategies before experimentation occurs. This unit provides essential knowledge about alcohol's physical and mental health effects, empowers pupils to resist peer pressure, and equips them with practical harm-reduction strategies. At this developmental stage, establishing informed attitudes towards alcohol supports safer decision-making throughout adolescence and into adulthood.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 7 that alcohol is a substance that affects the body and brain, and that it is illegal for people under 18 to buy or be sold alcohol in England.
Pupils should be familiar with peer pressure and refusal skills from previous units, recognising that making independent choices about risky substances is important for health and safety.
Pupils should know from earlier learning about the importance of making informed decisions for wellbeing, and understand that asking for help or advice when unsure is responsible behaviour.

388894843.name: Our changing bodies: How will my body change through puberty?
388894843.description: This unit explores the physical and emotional changes during puberty. Pupils learn about body development, understand and manage changing emotions, develop self-awareness skills, and learn about personal hygiene practices to maintain health during adolescence.
388894843.why: As Year 8 pupils are experiencing or approaching puberty, they need comprehensive understanding of the physical and emotional changes occurring in their bodies and minds. This unit explores puberty as a natural developmental process, explains bodily changes, and provides practical guidance for managing emotions and maintaining hygiene. At this stage, clear, accurate information helps pupils to navigate adolescence confidently.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 7 basic information about puberty as a natural process involving physical and emotional changes that happen at different times for different people.
Pupils should be familiar with talking about emotions using appropriate vocabulary from previous units, and recognise that feelings can change during adolescence as the body develops.
Pupils should know from earlier learning about basic hygiene practices such as washing regularly, and understand that personal care routines become more important during puberty.

228877097.name: Staying safe and healthy: Forced marriage, FGM, hymenoplasty & virginity testing
228877097.description: This unit addresses violence against women and girls, updated to reflect the 2026 RSHE guidance. Pupils learn about FGM, virginity testing, hymenoplasty and forced marriage, understanding the serious harms, legal protections, and how to seek help and report concerns.
228877097.why: As Year 8 pupils develop deeper understanding of consent, bodily autonomy and respectful relationships, they need safeguarding knowledge about harmful practices that violate these principles. This unit provides essential information about FGM, virginity testing, hymenoplasty and forced marriage as serious forms of abuse with legal protections. At this developmental stage, pupils can understand these complex issues sensitively, recognise warning signs, know how to seek help, and understand their role in protecting themselves and others from violence against women and girls.
prior: Pupils should understand what constitutes respectful relationships, including that everyone has the right to make decisions about their own body and future without coercion.
Pupils should be familiar with the concept of consent from earlier learning, recognising that all people deserve bodily autonomy and that forcing someone into harmful practices is abuse.
Pupils should know from earlier units how to report concerns to trusted adults and access support, understanding that reporting abuse protects both themselves and others.

214951912.name: Communities: How can we understand and respect different types of relationships?
214951912.description: This unit explores how to respect people in diverse relationships by examining the Equality Act 2010, the experiences of LGBT people in modern Britain, and the journey to marriage equality.
214951912.why: As Year 9 pupils develop a more sophisticated understanding of society and relationships, they learn about legal protections for partnerships and the progress towards LGBT equality. This unit builds on previous learning about respect and communities by examining sexual orientation as a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010.
prior: Pupils should understand from Key Stage 3 that everyone deserves respect regardless of protected characteristics, including sexual orientation, and discrimination is wrong.
Pupils should know from earlier learning about stereotypes and prejudice.

660696192.name: Healthy relationships: How do relationships change?
660696192.description: This unit explores different types of committed relationships, including romantic partnerships, marriage and civil partnerships. Pupils learn about the characteristics of healthy long-term relationships, legal rights and protections, and how relationships evolve over time.
660696192.why: As Year 9 pupils begin exploring romantic relationships and understanding long-term partnerships, they require accurate information about various types of committed relationships and their legal implications. This unit provides essential knowledge about marriage, civil partnerships, and cohabitation, clarifying legal protections and dispelling myths, such as 'common-law marriage'. At this stage, pupils can understand healthy romantic relationships and how partnerships develop, empowering them to build respectful and equitable relationships as they mature into young adulthood.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 7 and Year 8 the characteristics of positive relationships, including trust, respect, honesty and kindness, and how these apply to all relationship types.
Pupils should be familiar with concepts of consent and boundaries from previous units.
Pupils should know from earlier learning about different types of families and relationships in their communities.

444079318.name: Power in relationships: How can we keep safe?
444079318.description: This unit explores power dynamics, consent and safety in relationships. Pupils learn about consent in intimate relationships, recognise exploitation and grooming, understand what constitutes sexual harassment, and know how to seek help and report concerns.
444079318.why: As Year 9 pupils form increasingly independent romantic and social relationships, they need a sophisticated understanding of consent, power dynamics and exploitation to protect themselves and others. This unit provides essential safeguarding knowledge about sexual harassment, grooming and exploitative behaviours, empowering pupils to recognise warning signs and understand their rights. At this developmental stage, clear information about consent laws, boundaries, and reporting mechanisms enables pupils to establish safe and respectful relationships and seek help confidently.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 8 what constitutes consent and boundaries in relationships, including that consent must be freely given and can be withdrawn at any time.
Pupils should be familiar with power imbalances in relationships from previous units.
Pupils should know from earlier learning how to report concerns and access support, understanding that harmful behaviour is never the victim's fault and professional help is available.

429693785.name: Healthy intimate relationships: How can sex be safe?
429693785.description: This unit explores safe sexual practices, consent, contraception and sexual health. Pupils learn about healthy intimate relationships, contraceptive options including condoms, how to reduce STI risks, HIV prevention, and how to access sexual health services.
429693785.why: As pupils approach the age of sexual consent and become closer to the age where they might develop intimate relationships, they require accurate information about safe sex, contraception and sexual health. This unit provides essential knowledge about preventing STIs and unintended pregnancies, understanding consent in sexual contexts, and accessing confidential healthcare services. At this stage, evidence-based sex education helps to support pupils make informed, responsible decisions about their sexual health and establish respectful intimate relationships.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 8 the importance of consent in relationships, including that consent must be freely given, ongoing, and can be withdrawn at any time in any situation.
Pupils should be familiar with basic reproductive health and puberty changes from previous units.
Pupils should know from earlier learning how to access healthcare support.

111092213.name: Media influence: How can I look after myself?
111092213.description: This unit addresses online risks to wellbeing, including protecting personal information, understanding pornography's harmful influence on relationships, recognising online addiction and gambling harms, and responding to trolls and harassment whilst seeking appropriate support.
111092213.why: As Year 9 pupils may spend more time navigating the online world independently, they might be exposed to harmful content, including pornography, gambling and harassment. This unit provides essential critical thinking skills to evaluate online influences on their wellbeing, relationships and self-image. At this stage, pupils require education about pornography's unrealistic portrayals, gambling risks and the importance of protecting personal information. This helps ensure pupils make informed choices, recognise harmful behaviours, and seek support when necessary.
prior: Pupils should understand from Key Stage 3 basic online safety principles.
Pupils should be familiar with characteristics of healthy relationships from previous units.
Pupils should know from earlier learning how to report harmful online content and access support.

622162958.name: Physical health: What's so important about sleep?
622162958.description: This unit emphasises the importance of quality sleep for physical health, mental wellbeing and learning. Pupils explore how sleep affects their bodies and minds, understand the consequences of poor sleep, and develop practical strategies for establishing healthy sleep routines.
622162958.why: As Year 9 pupils face increasing academic pressures and screen time, many experience disrupted sleep during a critical period of development. This unit provides essential knowledge about the impact of sleep on growth, learning, mood, and mental health. At this stage, establishing healthy sleep routines is crucial for managing stress and maintaining academic performance. Understanding the relationship between screen use and sleep quality supports pupils to make informed choices that protect their wellbeing during adolescence.
prior: Pupils should understand from Key Stage 3 that sleep is essential for health and different people need different amounts, with teenagers typically requiring more sleep than adults.
Pupils should be familiar with basic healthy lifestyle concepts from previous units, recognising that physical activity, nutrition and sleep all contribute to development.
Pupils should know from earlier learning about the impact of screen time on wellbeing.

456910409.name: Risky substances: What do I need to know about illegal and prescription drugs?
456910409.description: Pupils learn which drugs are illegal, understand the effects of stimulants, depressants and hallucinogens, recognise links between drug use and mental health, and develop skills to stay safe. This unit includes includes content on the increased risk of potent synthetic drugs.
456910409.why: As Year 9 pupils gain independence, they require accurate, evidence-based information about drug classifications, risks and effects. This unit provides knowledge about the serious physical and mental health harms of illegal drugs, including potent synthetic drugs. At this developmental stage, pupils can understand the bidirectional relationship between drugs and mental health, and develop assertiveness skills to resist pressure.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 8 the risks associated with alcohol and tobacco, and have developed basic skills for resisting peer pressure around risky substances.
Pupils should be familiar with making safe decisions about risky substances from previous units, including understanding peer influence and pressure.
Pupils should know from earlier learning that illegal behaviours have consequences including criminal responsibility.

492904039.name: Staying safe and healthy: What do I need to know about basic first aid?
492904039.description: This unit teaches essential first aid skills for managing injuries and emergencies. Pupils learn to treat cuts, burns, fractures, sprains and stings, respond to heat imbalances, choking and anaphylaxis, and provide care for unconscious casualties confidently.
492904039.why: As Year 9 pupils gain greater independence in social situations, sports and activities, they require practical first aid skills to respond effectively to injuries and emergencies. This unit provides essential, potentially life-saving knowledge, including CPR and the use of defibrillators, empowering pupils to act confidently in critical situations. At this developmental stage, pupils can understand emergency protocols and develop the composure needed to provide effective first aid.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 8 basic treatment for minor ailments and common injuries, and know when professional medical help is needed rather than self-care.
upils should be familiar with emergency procedures from earlier learning, including how to call 999, provide clear information to emergency services, and stay calm in urgent situations.
Pupils should know from previous units about personal safety and risk management, understanding the importance of assessing situations carefully before taking action to help others.

357948769.name: Our changing bodies: When might I need to seek support?
357948769.description: This unit explores normal pubertal changes and when to seek help. Pupils learn about brain development during adolescence, understand menstrual health including how cycles change with age, recognise period problems, and know when and how to access professional support.
357948769.why: As Year 9 pupils experience ongoing pubertal changes, they need to distinguish between normal development and symptoms requiring medical attention. This unit provides essential knowledge about menstrual health conditions like endometriosis and PCOS, supporting pupils to recognise when professional help is needed.
prior: Pupils should understand from Key Stage 3 basic information about puberty and menstruation.
Pupils should be familiar with discussing physical and emotional changes using appropriate vocabulary. from previous units,.
Pupils should know from earlier learning about how to access healthcare support.

171270064.name: Staying safe: what do I need to know about knife crime?
171270064.description: This unit, aligned with the 2025 RSHE guidance, explores knife crime and legislation regarding weapons. Pupils learn about legal consequences, understand how online sources can glamorise and distort the realities of carrying knives, and recognise strategies to stay safe whilst accessing support.
171270064.why: In line with the 2026 RSHE statutory guidance, this unit covers knife crime. It builds on previous content about keeping safe in the community and how the media, including social media, can present a disorted version of society.
prior: Pupils should understand from Year 8 how to increase personal safety in public spaces and recognise situations that may present risks to themselves or others in their community.
Pupils should be familiar with online safety from previous units, recognising that some online content glamorises harmful behaviours.
Pupils should know from earlier learning how to access support from trusted adults.

908855761.name: Our community
908855761.outcome: I can describe what an inclusive community looks like and explain why it is important for a community to be inclusive.
points: We can be members of multiple communities.
Communities can be made up of a range of diverse people.
We have a responsibility to make communities welcoming and inclusive.
keywords: a group of people brought together by shared attitudes, interests, beliefs or location
involving people from a range of different backgrounds
taking care of or protecting something

points: Smoking introduces harmful and risky substances like tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide into the body.
Vapes contain ingredients found in everyday items, but when inhaled through a vape can be harmful to health.
Illegal vapes can be extremely dangerous and hard to spot.
keywords: an addictive drug that cigarettes and some vapes contain
a substance in tobacco smoke that can cause cancer and damage to the lungs
vapes sold illegally in the UK that may contain banned substances or unsafe levels of nicotine that can seriously harm a person's health
tips: Add localised support for young people surrounding smoking and vaping to the lesson and emphasise that pupils can speak to a trusted adult if they have concerns about their own or others' vaping or smoking habits.

739280101.outcome: I can describe the physical and social impacts of smoking, vaping and using nicotine products and explain how best to say no to peer pressure.
points: Smoking, vaping and using nicotine products are linked to serious health concerns.
Making healthy choices benefits physical and mental health; quitting smoking or vaping are examples of healthy choices.
Smoking, vaping and using nicotine products can impact a person socially.
Saying no assertively rather than aggressively can help challenge peer pressure safely and respectfully.
keywords: an addictive drug that cigarettes and some vapes contain

858787430.name: Getting support to give up smoking or vaping
858787430.outcome: I can describe what happens when someone quits smoking or vaping, and explain how support makes it easier to stop.
points: Quitting smoking or vaping helps the body recover and feel healthier.
Nicotine addiction can make quitting difficult, but support helps.
Using NHS or local stop-smoking services makes quitting more successful.
Cravings and mood changes are normal when giving up nicotine.
Trusted adults and professionals can guide and encourage quitting safely.

446095135.name: Menstrual health
446095135.outcome: I can describe the menstrual cycle and explain how to track cycles.
points: There are four phases in the menstrual cycle; the length of cycle depends on many factors.
Ovaries produce eggs which travel down the fallopian tubes to the womb or the uterus.
The endometrium thickens ready for a fertilised egg; when an egg isn’t fertilised, the endometrium is shed as a period.
Menstruation is different for all individuals and there is no ‘normal’.
People can track their menstrual cycles and that can be helpful for preparation.

498747459.outcome: I can describe what menstrual products are available and evaluate their suitability.

There are disposable and reusable menstrual products.
The menstrual cycle can affect other parts of the body.

579603191.outcome: I can describe how emotions might change linked to cycles and how to support a menstruating person.

Menstrual cycles change with time.
Menstruation is not dirty or shameful and anyone can talk about it.

201358106.name: The role of faith groups in a community
201358106.outcome: I can explain how faith contributes to a community and describe ways to respect different faiths.
points: Faith groups can play a significant role in building and maintaining community cohesion.
Respecting different faith groups involves understanding and valuing their contributions.
There are various ways to show respect to people of different faiths.
keywords: a person’s religion or set of beliefs
being considerate of others and the world around you; treating people fairly and how you would like to be treated
when things or people stick together to make a united group or whole

198147014.name: Faith and culture in modern Britain
198147014.outcome: I can describe the diversity of faiths and cultures in modern Britain, and explain their contributions to society.
points: Modern Britain is home to a diverse range of faiths and cultures.
Different faiths and cultures contribute positively to British society.
Diverse cultures and faiths can enrich communities.
Respect and tolerance are crucial in a diverse society.
keywords: including people or things from a range of different backgrounds or types
being considerate of others and the world around you; treating people fairly and how you would like to be treated

664060546.name: Prejudice and discrimination of faith and culture
664060546.outcome: I can explain the impact of prejudice and discrimination on individuals of different faith and culture.
points: Prejudice involves preconceived opinions, and is not based on reason or experience.
Discrimination is the unjust treatment of different categories of people.
Faith and culture are personal, and should be respected.
Prejudice and discrimination can have severe impacts on individuals and communities.
Challenging prejudice and discrimination safely is crucial for a fair and equal society.
keywords: when someone judges or dislikes others unfairly, without knowing them, based on things like race, gender or appearance

tips: Remind pupils that it is important for us to safely speak out against unfairness or any kind of discrimination, and draw their attention to policies in school to help them report incidents.

344732696.name: Making the world a more inclusive place
344732696.outcome: I can describe what inclusion looks like and explain how we can make the world a more inclusive place.
points: Every individual is unique, and these differences contribute to a richer, more vibrant community.
Everyone should feel respected, valued and have the same opportunities as others, regardless of their background.
Exclusion can have a negative impact on a person, for instance, poor mental health.
The British values help to promote a more inclusive society.
keywords: a time or situation that makes it possible to do something
actively making sure everyone belongs, can participate fully and is treated fairly, no matter their differences or backgrounds

558833996.name: Kindness in our community
558833996.outcome: I can explain why kindness and respect matter in our community and how my actions can positively impact others.
points: Treating others with kindness and respect helps create safer, more positive communities, including in public spaces.
Everyone has equal rights under the law regardless of their background.
We all have a responsibility to treat people fairly.
Understanding how our words and actions impact others helps prevent harm and promotes inclusion.
keywords: being nice, caring and thinking about how others feel
the state of being equal, especially in status, rights and opportunities
being considerate of others and the world around you; treating people fairly and how you would like to be treated
tips: Use examples from everyday life, such as holding doors open, respecting personal space, or speaking politely to staff in shops, to make the concept of kindness in public spaces concrete and relatable for pupils.

872962804.name: Keeping safe in our community
872962804.outcome: I can explain how to stay safe in public spaces, to trust my instincts and to seek help or report harmful behaviour.
points: We can use personal safety strategies in public spaces, such as staying alert and being aware of our surroundings.
Trusting instincts is an important way of recognising when a situation doesn’t feel right.
There are places and people you can ask for help in public spaces and ways to report harmful behaviour.
Taking steps to increase safety does not mean someone is at fault if they experience harmful behaviour.
keywords: steps taken in advance to keep yourself or others safe from harm
tips: Speak to your RSHE lead or Designated Safeguarding Lead (DSL) before teaching this lesson. You may decide to provide information on local safe places or support networks specific to your area (e.g., police community support officers, helplines, etc).

754869578.name: Bullying
754869578.outcome: I can explain what the difference between bullying and banter are and where bullying can happen.
points: Bullying is intentional, repetitive behaviour which is intended to hurt someone emotionally or physically.
Banter can become bullying if it is repetitive and clearly upsets the victim.
The four main types of bullying are emotional, physical, cyber and social.
Bullying can happen anywhere.

269884112.outcome: I can explain the impact of bullying on the victim, the perpetrator, and those around.

Bullying can create a culture of fear for everyone involved.

425869295.name: How to stop bullying
425869295.outcome: I can explain different ways of stopping bullying and evaluate their effectiveness.
points: If faced with bullying, try not to react to the bully, do your best to ignore it and report it to a trusted adult.
Bullying someone back is never an acceptable way to deal with bullying.
Block or report accounts that are engaging in cyberbullying and tell a trusted adult.
There are lots of sites available for support and guidance around bullying, including Childline.

64665040.name: Harmful sexual behaviour
64665040.outcome: I can describe what harmful sexual behaviour is, explain the law around it and explain where to get support.
points: Harmful sexual behaviour (HSB) is inappropriate sexual behaviour which is harmful and abusive.
Sexual violence can escalate and begin as sexist jokes or comments.
90% of girls and nearly 50% of boys have been sent explicit pictures or videos of things they did not want to see.
There are laws to protect people from harmful sexual behaviour.
Harmful sexual behaviour can take different forms, including: harassment, upskirting, coercion and manipulation.
keywords: unwanted words, actions or behaviours of a sexual nature that make someone uncomfortable, upset or afraid
tips: You may want to work with your RSHE or DSL lead to adapt this lesson to the needs of your school and community before delivery.

If something online feels wrong or uncomfortable, it's important to tell a trusted adult.

430595352.name: How I spend my time online
430595352.outcome: I can explain the importance of managing my time online effectively.
points: We all have unique ways of enjoying the online world.
Online activities include socialising, watching videos, playing games, learning and working.
Some online activities are healthy in the long-term, some are entertaining, and some are harmful.
Getting a healthy balance of fun, social, learning, creative and work activities is important, both online and offline.
keywords: to talk, play, or spend time with friends, family or new people

651461753.name: Time online and sleep
651461753.outcome: I can describe ways to manage my time online and keep a healthy sleep schedule.
points: Blue light is produced by electronic screens and disturbs sleeping patterns.
Disturbed sleep can impact our physical wellbeing.
Not using screens at least one hour before bed can help us to sleep.

a natural chemical in your body that helps control sleep by making you feel sleepy when it gets dark

tips: It could be useful for teachers to show pupils how to switch on 'night mode' on digital devices. This reduces blue light emissions which can reduce the melatonin supression when using devices before bed. However, be clear that this is not a 'fix' for pupils using screens before bed.

598829078.name: Time online and body image
598829078.outcome: I can explain how people online may alter their appearance and why this is not representative of how I should look.
points: Many celebrities and influencers use filters to edit their appearance.
Comparing ourselves to people online is comparing ourselves to an impossible ideal.
We should not expect ourselves or others to look like people we see online.
Everybody is different.
Body shaming online or in person is never acceptable.
keywords: an effect used on a photo or video to alter the way you look
how we see, think or feel about our body, including our shape, size and appearance
to make hurtful comments about a person's appearance, body shape or size
tips: Body shaming someone is never ok, and judgements about a person's value and worth should never be based on their physical appearance. When influencers and celebrities use filters, it is often to hide their own insecurities.

836449232.outcome: I can describe ways that social media can impact my self-esteem.

People may act differently online than they do in person.
The number of online friends or likes someone has does not determine their worth.

440194898.name: Time online and learning
440194898.outcome: I can explain how my time online can impact my learning.
points: Watching lots of short form videos can affect our attention span.
It can take up to 20 minutes to refocus on learning after engaging in an online activity, like browsing social media.
Some sites can benefit learning, but regular screen breaks should be taken if using digital devices.

a chemical in the body that gives us a short-term feeling of reward

872977440.name: Planning time online
872977440.outcome: I can explain how to plan my time online effectively.
points: Using a diary or organiser can help plan time after school or work.
It is important to be offline long enough to sleep, socialise, learn and exercise.
It is better to put activities that benefit our health, wellbeing and learning first.
Using 'Do Not Disturb', setting limits on social media and not using devices at meal times can limit screen time.

to decide which task is most important and requires attention first

392247322.name: Online bullying
392247322.outcome: I can explain what online bullying is.
points: Online bullying is often linked to discrimination.
Discrimination could be about any of the protected characteristics, as well as lifestyle choices and financial status.
Online bullying can take the form of threats, harassment, humiliation, cyberstalking, exclusion or impersonation.
Online bullying can take place anywhere online.
keywords: when people are treated unfairly or differently because of things like their race, gender or beliefs
when someone repeatedly bothers, bullies, or disturbs another person, making them feel unsafe, uncomfortable or upset
making someone feel embarrassed, ashamed or unimportant
being purposefully left out of a group
tips: Online bullying often involves discrimination and/or hate speech and online bullies are often more emboldened to spread bigoted views online than they are in-person. 26262911.name: Responding to online bullying
26262911.outcome: I can explain what to do if I witness online bullying.
points: It is good to be an active bystander in order to reduce online bullying.
It is not acceptable to ignore online bullying if we witness it.
We can report our concerns to the website or app that we are using.
We can report our concerns to trusted adults and the police.

points: There are many motivations to take part in online bullying.
Some people are insecure and look to put other people down.
Some people enjoy being hurtful to others.
Some people are passive bystanders, who say nothing when they witness bullying.
Some people don't realise how much they've upset someone if they are unkind online.

894536674.outcome: I can explain what knife crime is, how it is misrepresented online, and where to get help if I’m worried about violence.
points: Knife crime is rare but has serious consequences for individuals and communities.
Most young people do not carry knives.
Carrying a knife often increases the risk of harm to yourself.
Online content can glamorise violence or distort reality, making knife crime appear more common than it is.
There is support and advice available for young people worried about violence or knife crime.
keywords: any crime that involves a knife, including carrying, threatening with, or using it illegally
to make something harmful or dangerous seem attractive or exciting, often in media or online
to change or twist something away from its normal or true form
tips: You should speak to your RSHE lead or DSL before teaching this lesson. Make it clear where pupils can report concerns or seek support in your educational setting and local community.

880924790.name: The laws about knives and weapons
880924790.outcome: I can explain the law on knives and weapons.
points: It is illegal to carry a knife or offensive weapon without a reasonable excuse, even if you don’t intend to use it.
The law covers a wide range of weapons, not just knives (for example, items that are disguised as everyday objects).
Online sales of knives and weapons are regulated, but attempting to buy or sell illegally is also a crime.
Weapon-related crime and possession carries serious consequences.
keywords: a breach of a law or rule; an illegal act
having something that belongs to you or is under your control, such as keeping an item, weapon or other object with you or in your care
tips: Emphasise that laws are there to keep everyone safe. Be prepared to signpost pupils to support if they express concerns about their own safety or that of others.

866458891.name: The consequences of knife crime
866458891.outcome: I can explain the consequences of knife crime for individuals and communities and how it impacts future choices.
points: Knife crime can have legal, physical and emotional consequences for everyone involved.
Victims, perpetrators, families and communities are all affected by knife crime.
Being involved in knife crime can affect future education, employment and travel opportunities.
Healthy, positive decision-making reduces risks and promotes safer communities.

an individual who has committed a harmful act
